title: Hera asteroid images: three ways to study Didymos

content:
AFC, HyperScout H and TIRI capture different clues about the asteroid pair; ESA scheduled a detailed-image briefing for November 25.

November 18, 2026

Key points

  1. 01

    Hera’s AFC, HyperScout H and TIRI provide monochrome, multispectral and thermal-infrared observations.

  2. 02

    HyperScout H observes 25 hues, while AFC’s described image has a spatial resolution of about 2.7 meters per pixel.

  3. 03

    ESA reports boulder-rich areas and possible landslide traces near Didymos’s central ridge; the suggested role of its rapid rotation remains tentative.

  4. 04

    ESA scheduled a detailed-image briefing for November 25, 2026, in Berlin or online, with registration by November 23.

In this article

  1. 01 What each Hera instrument observes
  2. 02 What Hera’s observations show about Didymos
  3. 03 Why TIRI can show Dimorphos across its extent
  4. 04 When ESA scheduled the detailed-image briefing

Hera combines monochrome, multispectral and thermal views of Didymos and Dimorphos. ESA scheduled its detailed-image briefing for November 25, 2026.

ESA says Hera is observing Didymos and its moonlet Dimorphos with three complementary instruments: a monochrome camera, a multispectral imager and a thermal-infrared camera. Each records a different kind of information about the asteroids. In its November 17 account of Hera’s observations, the European Space Agency (ESA) also described detailed images as scheduled for presentation on November 25, 2026.

What each Hera instrument observes

AFC records surface features in monochrome; HyperScout H measures reflected light across 25 hues; and TIRI maps thermal infrared. ESA says those different observations can help researchers examine surface shape, composition clues and material properties.

InstrumentObservation modeWhat it can help researchers study
Asteroid Framing Camera (AFC)Monochrome images for navigation and scientific observation; approximately 2.7 meters per pixel for the described imageSurface features such as boulders and clearer areas
HyperScout H25 hues, from visible red into near-infraredSpectral signatures associated with composition, compared with laboratory measurements of meteorites and minerals
Thermal Infrared Imager (TIRI)Thermal-infrared imaging; supplied and operated by the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA)Temperature patterns that can help distinguish solid, porous or broken rock from loose material such as dust

ESA’s phrase “superhuman vision” refers to the combined reach of these three observation modes. HyperScout H’s spectral measurements offer clues about composition, while TIRI’s temperature patterns help researchers investigate surface materials; neither is simply another version of AFC’s monochrome view.

Read the three views as complementary evidence: surface detail, spectral clues and temperature patterns each answer a different question.

What Hera’s observations show about Didymos

ESA describes boulder-rich and clearer areas on Didymos, along with traces that might be landslides near the asteroid’s central ridge. Patrick Michel, Hera’s principal investigator, says Didymos rotates once every 2.2 hours and suggests that its rapid spin might encourage material to migrate toward the equator, helping form the ridge. That is a possible explanation, not a settled conclusion.

ESA gives Didymos’s diameter as 780 meters and Dimorphos’s as 151 meters. NeoTeo previously covered an earlier close-up of Didymos, a separate view from this account of Hera’s three observation modes.

Why TIRI can show Dimorphos across its extent

ESA says Dimorphos is almost entirely in shadow in the other images described, while TIRI’s thermal-infrared image shows the moonlet across its full extent. TIRI’s temperature mapping gives researchers another way to examine the surface alongside the light-based observations.

NASA’s DART spacecraft struck Dimorphos on September 26, 2022. Hera’s investigation is examining questions about the impact’s effects on the asteroid’s shape, composition and structure.

When ESA scheduled the detailed-image briefing

ESA announced a briefing for November 25, 2026, in Berlin or online, with registration by November 23. Those arrangements appeared in an ESA post dated November 16.
